title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Wixom backs zoning limits on a big project; what it signals for bills, water and other towns.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're looking at Wixom's narrow council vote on new zoning rules aimed at reining in noise and utility costs from a proposed hyperscale project.
That 4-3 decision today really stood out. Graham, walk us through what happened in Oakland County.

The council advanced changes during the ongoing 180-day moratorium for a 600,000-square-foot facility on 54 acres. Residents had raised alarms about power demand, water use, and noise that could push up household electric bills.
Why does a single township vote like this carry weight beyond Wixom's borders?
It sets a potential template for other Michigan communities facing similar proposals. We've seen parallel debates in Ingham, Jackson, Washtenaw, and Cass counties this week alone.
So the bigger story here is local pushback against rapid data center growth and its ripple effects on everyday residents.
Exactly. These facilities need enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and when they connect to the grid, costs can spread to nearby ratepayers even 30 or 60 miles away.
How long has this tension been building in places like Wixom?
The moratorium gave the council time to study the impacts after residents organized around the specific project. The 4-3 vote shows the divide is real but the majority wants stricter guardrails.
What specific changes are they advancing on noise and costs?
New zoning language targets noise levels and utility cost allocation so the data center doesn't shift burdens onto regular households through higher bills or strained infrastructure.
And how does this connect to the water rules the state tightened yesterday?

Michigan posted updated tracking for Great Lakes basin withdrawals. Projects needing millions of gallons daily for cooling now face clearer limits, and Wixom's concerns line up with that statewide shift.
Farmland conversion is another angle here with 54 acres involved. What does that mean for the area long term?
Losing productive land to industrial use changes the local tax base and character of the township. Councils are weighing that against potential economic benefits from the project.
Who are the main players pushing back versus supporting the development?
Residents and some council members focused on protecting bills and quality of life. The developer side wants to move forward under the new rules once the moratorium lifts.
What happens next in Wixom after this vote?
The changes head toward final adoption while the moratorium continues, giving everyone more time to review the 600,000-square-foot plan against the tighter standards.
Does this make similar projects harder elsewhere or just smarter?
It raises the bar for transparency on costs and impacts. Other towns watching Mason and Cass County debates may borrow from Wixom's approach.
Let's shift to Mason for a moment. What's happening there tomorrow?
The city council resumes debate on a hyperscale proposal in nearby Vevay Township plus possible updates to the citizen-initiated noise ordinance.
That ties directly into the tax fight mentioned in Ingham and Jackson counties.
Residents are watching how much these facilities will pay in taxes and how that affects both household bills and local budgets if the projects advance.
Now turning to the attorney general's actions yesterday. What exactly is Dana Nessel seeking?
She's asking the Court of Appeals to reopen review of secret DTE contracts tied to the OpenAI/Oracle project in Saline Township, arguing ratepayers deserve to see the terms.
Why is transparency on those contracts so important for electric bills?
Hidden deals could mean ratepayers absorb unexpected costs or lose out on tax revenue. The case could influence how future projects get approved statewide.
Saline Township also hired a retired sergeant for zoning fights. What does that signal?
They're preparing for more complex industrial proposals, including potential data centers, and want a dedicated point person for residents near Ann Arbor.
Over in Cass County yesterday, residents packed a hall. What were the main worries?
Save Cass County drew a standing-room crowd concerned about noise, water use, and rising electric bills from proposed facilities. They're urging officials to reject or restrict projects.
And that Dowagiac lawsuit from yesterday involves nonstop noise from a former crypto site.
Neighbors say the high-pitched whine from the Alliance Cloud Services operation violates the city's new noise limits and forces them indoors.
How does all this add up for communities 30 miles from any single project?
Grid connections mean rate impacts can spread regionally, which is why so many townships are acting now on zoning and noise before more land gets optioned.
Graham, any sense of how many places have paused or tightened rules recently?
At least a handful across Oakland, Ingham, Jackson, Washtenaw, and Cass counties have active moratoriums or new ordinances under discussion this week.
What should listeners watch for in the coming days?
Tomorrow's meetings will show whether the Wixom model spreads or if different communities take their own approaches.
Let's move to On Deck. What's on the calendar for Monday?
Mason City Council meets to continue the data center zoning ordinance revisions and noise standards discussion.
Coldwater has a joint session with the planning commission and board of public utilities.
That meeting covers data center impacts on zoning, energy use, neighborhoods, and possible new ordinances.
Caledonia Township Planning Commission is also discussing its data center ordinance and a potential moratorium extension.
Kalamazoo City Commission will vote on a resolution for a temporary moratorium on data center development.
Those are all actionable for listeners who want to attend or comment.
Exactly. Agendas are public and the issues affect bills and land use directly.
Any final thoughts on the pattern we're seeing?
Communities are demanding more say on costs and side effects before projects scale up. The Wixom vote is one clear example of that push.
It feels like a turning point where local rules are catching up to the pace of proposals.
We'll keep tracking how these play out across the state.
Thanks for breaking it down tonight, Graham.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Wixom's Close Vote Tightens Data Center Rules Amid Power and Water Worries
